description:
We are Lucky Bits, a passionate team of students interested in technology, innovation, and space exploration. Our team focuses on combining creativity, problem-solving, and technical skills to develop innovative solutions for real-world challenges.

We are interested in software development, web development, artificial intelligence, machine learning, and data analysis. Through the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we aim to explore Earth-related challenges, collaborate, learn new technologies.
summary:
EARTHSONIQ – Turning Earth's Visual Data into Sound

EARTHSONIQ, developed by Team Lucky Bits, is an interactive accessibility platform that transforms NASA Earth Information Center (EIC) visualizations into real-time soundscapes. It uses computer vision techniques to analyze image features such as brightness, motion, edge gradients, and visual complexity, converting them into dynamic audio through Web Audio and Tone.js synthesis.

The platform features an interactive 3D Earth with 11 exploration points, real-time audio visualization, before-and-after comparisons, historical environmental timelines, and an AI-powered Earth Assistant. It also supports voice navigation, audio descriptions, downloadable WAV files, and scientific data provenance indicators.

EARTHSONIQ addresses the challenge by making complex Earth science more accessible to blind, low-vision, and sensory-diverse communities through an alternative auditory experience. By transforming visual patterns into meaningful sound, it helps users explore environmental changes through listening rather than relying only on sight.

Our goal is to make Earth's changing systems more inclusive, interactive, and understandable, ensuring that everyone can experience and explore our planet's vital signs.
details:
Project Details – EARTHSONIQ

EARTHSONIQ, developed by Team Lucky Bits, is an interactive web-based platform that transforms NASA Earth Information Center (EIC) visualizations into real-time soundscapes. It helps users experience Earth's environmental changes through sound instead of relying only on visual information.

How Does It Work?

EARTHSONIQ processes sequential Earth visualization frames using computer vision techniques. It extracts four important visual features: luminance (brightness), optical flow (movement), spatial edge gradients (boundaries and patterns), and Shannon entropy (visual complexity). These features control a dynamic audio synthesis engine built with Web Audio API and Tone.js, generating unique sounds based on the visual data without using pre-recorded audio loops.

Benefits and Intended Impact

The platform improves accessibility for blind, low-vision, and sensory-diverse communities. It provides an alternative way to explore environmental patterns, understand changes over time, and experience complex Earth science through sound. It also encourages inclusive scientific learning and makes Earth observation more interactive.

Tools and Technologies Used

  • Frontend: React, HTML, CSS, JavaScript
  • Audio Processing: Web Audio API, Tone.js
  • Visual Processing: Computer Vision and image feature extraction
  • 3D Visualization: WebGL and Canvas
  • Accessibility: Web Speech API, voice recognition, and keyboard navigation
  • Data Analysis: FFT spectrum analysis and Shannon entropy
  • Platform: Web-based interactive application

Creativity and Innovation

EARTHSONIQ combines Earth science, computer vision, audio synthesis, and accessibility in one platform. Its advanced features include an interactive 3D Earth with 11 mission pins, a 64-band real-time audio analyzer, historical timeline exploration from 1992 to 2026, before-and-after comparisons, and an AI-powered Earth Assistant. Users can also export synthesized audio as 16-bit, 44.1 kHz stereo WAV files and download scientific audit reports.

Factors Considered by Our Team

Our team considered accessibility, scientific accuracy, meaningful sound mapping, user interaction, and usability. We included scientific provenance indicators to distinguish physically measured sensor information from visual estimates or model proxies. We also focused on generating genuine dynamic audio rather than relying on repetitive background sounds.

Our ultimate goal is to make Earth's changing systems accessible to everyone by turning complex planetary visualizations into an inclusive auditory experience.
